title: The Bat Had Been Shouting
paragraphs: A small bat hunting over a pond may catch hundreds of insects in a night too dark for a person to see a hand held before the face.
Its eyes play almost no part in any of it.
The explanation, that the bat shouts and listens for the echoes, is now taught to schoolchildren, but it took roughly 150 years to travel from a strong suspicion to an accepted fact.
The story of that delay is, to my mind, as instructive as the biology, because the answer was essentially in hand in the 1790s and nobody could hear it.
The first careful experiments were made in 1793 and 1794 by Lazzaro Spallanzani, an Italian priest and professor at the University of Pavia.
He began with an owl, which flew well in dim light but struck the walls once the room was fully dark.
Bats, by contrast, flew freely in total darkness, so he blinded several, covering their eyes or removing them outright.
The blinded animals still swerved around obstacles and flew off, and some that he later recaptured had stomachs full of freshly caught insects.
Whatever guided them, it was not sight.
The next step came from Geneva, where the surgeon and naturalist Louis Jurine learned of the work and, in 1794, plugged the ears of bats with wax.
Deafened in this way, the animals blundered into obstacles they had cleared minutes earlier, and when the plugs came out they flew normally again.
Spallanzani repeated the experiment and confirmed it, concluding that the ears were somehow doing the work of the eyes, though he could not say how, since a flying bat seemed to make no sound at all.
The idea found few takers.
In 1800 the French anatomist Georges Cuvier judged the ear experiments unconvincing and proposed instead that the thin skin of the wings felt the air pushed back from nearby objects.
Cuvier's authority was enormous, and the touch theory held the field for more than a century.
Writers sometimes tell this as a tale of arrogance, and I think that is a little unfair: in 1800, a sense built on an inaudible sound was a hard thing to believe in.
Two guesses in the early twentieth century came closer.

In 1912, shortly after the Titanic struck an iceberg, the inventor Hiram Maxim suggested that bats sensed obstacles with low-frequency sound from their wingbeats, below the range of human hearing, and proposed a similar device for ships.
In 1920 the English physiologist Hamilton Hartridge argued the reverse: that bats emitted sounds above the range of human hearing and steered by their echoes.
Hartridge had the physics right, but he had no instrument that could detect such sounds, and the suggestion sat in the literature untested for nearly two decades.
The instrument turned up at Harvard.
The physicist George W. Pierce had built an apparatus that made high-frequency sound audible, and he was using it to study the songs of insects.
In 1938 Donald Griffin, then an undergraduate who had been banding bats to study their migrations, carried a cage of them into Pierce's laboratory.
Held in front of the detector, the silent-seeming animals were producing a torrent of sound far above the roughly 20 kilohertz ceiling of human hearing.
Griffin and Robert Galambos, a graduate student working on hearing, then ran the decisive tests.
They strung fine wires across a darkened room and counted how often flying bats touched them.
Bats whose mouths were tied shut, and bats whose ears were plugged, struck the wires far more often than untouched animals.
The results were published in 1941, and in 1944 Griffin coined a word for the sense: echolocation.
The physics explains why the sounds have to be so high.
Sound moves through air at about 340 meters per second, so a 50 kilohertz call has a wavelength of roughly 7 millimeters, and sound reflects cleanly only from objects at least about that size.
A mosquito or a fine wire is invisible to a low note and vivid to a high one.
The price is range.
Air absorbs high frequencies far more strongly than low ones, so the higher a bat pitches its call, the sooner the echo fades into silence.
Every species therefore lives with a trade, sharper detail for shorter reach, and most bats first detect a small insect only a few meters away.
Distance itself comes from timing: an echo from a target 1.7 meters away returns 10 milliseconds after the call, and the bat judges that gap closely enough to catch an insect in flight.
Call design varies, and two broad patterns stand out.
Many bats use frequency-modulated calls: brief sweeps that start high and plunge downward through a wide band of pitches in a few thousandths of a second.
Horseshoe bats, which emit through their nostrils past a fleshy nose-leaf, do something different.
They hold a long, nearly constant note, a little above 80 kilohertz in the greater horseshoe bat, and listen for small changes in the pitch of the echo.
The changes come from the Doppler shift, the effect that raises the pitch of an approaching siren: an echo from something the bat is flying toward comes back higher than the note it sent.

In 1968 Hans-Ulrich Schnitzler showed that a flying horseshoe bat lowers its outgoing note by just enough that the raised echo lands at the frequency where its hearing is sharpest, a trick now called Doppler shift compensation.
A hunt can be read off a recording.
While searching, a bat calls perhaps ten times a second.
Once it detects prey the rate climbs, and in the last fraction of a second before contact it rises to as many as 200 calls per second, a burst that researchers call the feeding buzz.
The calls are not whispers; the loudest species exceed 110 decibels close to the mouth, which raises an obvious problem, since the bat must hear a faint echo a moment after shouting.
A small muscle in the middle ear contracts just before each call, damping the ear's sensitivity, and relaxes within milliseconds so that the echo arrives at an ear that is open again.
A sound that loud is also a broadcast, and some of the intended victims are listening.
In the late 1950s Kenneth Roeder and Asher Treat showed that many night-flying moths carry a pair of simple ears on the thorax, each with only two sound-sensitive cells.
The more sensitive cell begins firing when a bat is still tens of meters away, well before the bat can detect the moth, and the moth responds by turning and flying directly away.

The second cell fires only when the sound grows loud, meaning the bat is close, and that sets off something quite different: the moth folds its wings and drops, or breaks into loops and spirals that no echo can predict.
Roeder worked much of this out with a loudspeaker and a floodlight in a field at night, and I admire the plainness of it: cheap equipment and patience exposed a contest no one had suspected.
A few moths do more than listen.
Tiger moths carry a pair of tymbals, ridged plates on the thorax that buckle and snap back, and when a bat closes in, some species answer with bursts of ultrasonic clicks.
In 1965 Dorothy Dunning and Roeder played recorded clicks to bats trained to catch mealworms tossed into the air, and the bats veered away from food they would otherwise have taken.
Three explanations have been offered, and they are not exclusive.

The clicks might simply startle a bat; they might warn it, since many tiger moths feed as caterpillars on plants that leave them foul-tasting; or they might jam its sonar by cluttering the moment when the echo is due.

In 2007 Jesse Barber and William Conner found support for the warning idea: bats learned to avoid clicking moths that tasted bad, and then avoided palatable moths that clicked as well, an acoustic form of mimicry.

In 2009 Aaron Corcoran, with Barber and Conner, showed that one species, Bertholdia trigona, clicks up to about 4,500 times per second, and that big brown bats attacking it kept trying and kept missing, a pattern that fits jamming rather than warning or startle.
It is tempting to call all of this an arms race, and the metaphor is useful, but I distrust how neat it makes things.
Plenty of eared moths are eaten anyway, and the clicking tiger moths are a small minority.
What the history shows more clearly than any metaphor is how much a science depends on its instruments.
Spallanzani and Jurine had the right answer within reach in 1794, and it waited until a physicist built a device for listening to insects.
The bat had been shouting the whole time.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Spallanzani's experiment with an owl showed that the owl
choices: could navigate in total darkness as well as any bat
relied on its ears rather than its eyes to avoid walls
flew well in dim light but hit the walls in full darkness
refused to fly at all once the room was fully dark
caught insects in the dark as long as its eyes were uncovered

proof.quote: flew well in dim light but struck the walls once the room was fully dark

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says the owl flew well in dim light but struck the walls once the room was fully dark. That contrast with the bats is what sent Spallanzani further.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 2 says the owl struck the walls in full darkness while the bats flew freely.
Wrong animal: the ear finding belongs to the bats in paragraph 3, not to the owl.
Too strong: the owl flew, and the passage says it struck the walls, not that it refused to fly.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about the owl catching insects.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of Spallanzani EXCEPT:
choices: He first plugged bats' ears with wax.
He held a professorship at Pavia.
He removed or covered the eyes of several bats.
He recaptured blinded bats with full stomachs.
He confirmed Jurine's result by repeating it.

proof.quote: professor at the University of Pavia
covering their eyes or removing them outright
some that he later recaptured had stomachs full of freshly caught insects
Spallanzani repeated the experiment and confirmed it
Louis Jurine learned of the work and, in 1794, plugged the ears of bats with wax

questions.why: Paragraph 3 gives the wax plugs to Louis Jurine of Geneva; Spallanzani repeated that experiment afterward. Pavia, the blinding, the recaptured bats, and the confirmation are all in paragraphs 2 and 3.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 2 calls him a professor at the University of Pavia.
Paragraph 2 says he covered the bats' eyes or removed them outright.
Paragraph 2 says some recaptured bats had stomachs full of freshly caught insects.
Paragraph 3 says Spallanzani repeated Jurine's experiment and confirmed it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, when Jurine plugged the ears of bats with wax, the bats
choices: flew normally but stopped catching insects
made audible sounds for the first time
struck walls only when the room was also dark
collided with obstacles they had just avoided
refused to leave the ground until the plugs were removed

proof.quote: blundered into obstacles they had cleared minutes earlier

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says the deafened bats blundered into obstacles they had cleared minutes earlier, and flew normally again once the plugs came out.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: paragraph 3 says nothing about the plugged bats' feeding, and they did not fly normally.
Reversed: paragraph 3 says a flying bat seemed to make no sound at all.
Mash-up: the dark room and the wall belong to the owl in paragraph 2.
Too strong: paragraph 3 says the bats flew and blundered into obstacles; it never says they stayed on the ground.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 3, the word 'field' most nearly means
choices: an open stretch of farmland
the dominant position in a dispute
a branch of scientific study
the area a sense can reach
the ground on which a battle is fought

proof.quote: the touch theory held the field for more than a century

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says the touch theory held the field for more than a century right after noting Cuvier's enormous authority. To hold the field here is to remain the accepted view in the dispute.
distractorNotes: This is the everyday meaning of the word, but no land is involved in the sentence.
A field of study is a tempting reading, but the sentence says a theory held the field against rivals, not that it was a discipline.
The sentence is about a theory's standing, not about how far a sense reaches.
The idiom comes from battle, but the sentence describes a scientific debate, not combat.

questions.stem: The author discusses Maxim and Hartridge in paragraph 4 primarily to
choices: credit Maxim with the first correct account of how bats avoid obstacles
explain how the sinking of the Titanic led directly to the discovery of echolocation
contrast a physiologist's careful reasoning with an inventor's reckless guess
show that Cuvier's touch theory had been abandoned by 1912
show that the correct idea surfaced before an instrument could test it

proof.quote: Two guesses in the early twentieth century came closer.
he had no instrument that could detect such sounds, and the suggestion sat in the literature untested

questions.why: Paragraph 4 opens by saying two guesses came closer and closes by saying Hartridge's correct idea sat untested for nearly two decades because no instrument could detect the sounds. The paragraph is a bridge from suspicion to the instrument.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 4 says Hartridge, not Maxim, had the physics right.
Too strong: the Titanic prompted Maxim's suggestion, but paragraph 5 credits the discovery to a detector built for insect songs.
Outside the passage: the author never calls Maxim's guess reckless, and both men are presented as guessing.
Outside the passage: paragraph 4 never says the touch theory had been given up.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that bats seemed silent to Spallanzani and Jurine because
choices: the bats they studied called only while hunting insects outdoors
bats produce sound only when their eyes are covered
the wax plugs muffled the sounds the bats produced
the bats fell quiet whenever they were handled by people
the calls were pitched above the range of human hearing

proof.quote: a flying bat seemed to make no sound at all
far above the roughly 20 kilohertz ceiling of human hearing

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says a flying bat seemed to make no sound, and paragraph 5 reveals why: the sound was far above the roughly 20 kilohertz ceiling of human hearing. Put the two together and the silence was in the listeners, not the bats.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: nothing suggests the bats called only outdoors; paragraph 5 says they called in a laboratory.
Outside the passage: the calls had nothing to do with whether the eyes were covered.
Reversed: the plugs went in the bats' ears, not their mouths, and the bats seemed silent even without plugs.
Outside the passage: paragraph 5 shows handled bats calling in front of the detector.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in Griffin and Galambos's wire experiments, which bats struck the wires far more often than untouched animals?
choices: Those with their mouths tied shut and those with their ears plugged
Those with their eyes covered and those with their ears plugged
Those flying in a lighted room and those flying in a fully darkened one
Those with their mouths tied shut and those with their eyes covered
Those held in front of the detector and those released in the room

proof.quote: Bats whose mouths were tied shut, and bats whose ears were plugged, struck the wires far more often than untouched animals.

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says bats whose mouths were tied shut, and bats whose ears were plugged, struck the wires far more often than untouched animals: silencing the call or deafening the ear both broke the sense.
distractorNotes: Half right: plugged ears is one group, but paragraph 5 names tied mouths, not covered eyes, as the other.
Outside the passage: paragraph 5 describes only a darkened room.
Half right: tied mouths is one group, but the other had plugged ears; covered eyes belong to Spallanzani in paragraph 2.
Wrong detail: the detector in paragraph 5 revealed the calls; it was not a wire-test condition.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of Donald Griffin EXCEPT:
choices: He banded bats as an undergraduate to study their migrations.
He carried bats into Pierce's laboratory in 1938.
He built the apparatus that first detected the bats' calls.
He published the wire experiments with Galambos in 1941.
He coined the word echolocation in 1944.

proof.quote: an undergraduate who had been banding bats to study their migrations
carried a cage of them into Pierce's laboratory
Griffin and Robert Galambos, a graduate student working on hearing, then ran the decisive tests.
The results were published in 1941, and in 1944 Griffin coined a word for the sense: echolocation.
The physicist George W. Pierce had built an apparatus

questions.why: Paragraph 5 credits the detector to the physicist George W. Pierce, who built it to study insect songs; Griffin only carried the bats into the laboratory. The other four statements are all in paragraph 5.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 5 says Griffin had been banding bats to study their migrations as an undergraduate.
Paragraph 5 says he carried a cage of bats into Pierce's laboratory in 1938.
Paragraph 5 says Griffin and Galambos ran the tests and the results were published in 1941.
Paragraph 5 says that in 1944 Griffin coined the word echolocation.

questions.stem: According to the passage, raising the pitch of an echolocation call
choices: lets the call travel farther before its echo fades
reveals smaller objects but shortens the call's reach
lowers the speed at which the sound travels through air
makes the echo return sooner from a target at a given distance
increases the wavelength so fine wires reflect it more cleanly

proof.quote: the higher a bat pitches its call, the sooner the echo fades into silence
sharper detail for shorter reach

questions.why: Paragraph 6 lays out the trade: a short wavelength makes a fine wire vivid, but air absorbs high frequencies faster, so the echo fades sooner. Sharper detail for shorter reach.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 6 says the higher the pitch, the sooner the echo fades.
Outside the passage: the speed of sound in paragraph 6 is given as a constant, not something pitch changes.
Wrong mechanism: paragraph 6 ties echo timing to distance, not to pitch.
Reversed: paragraph 6 pairs the 50 kilohertz call with a short wavelength, and higher pitch means a shorter wave.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Schnitzler showed in 1968 that a flying horseshoe bat
choices: raises its outgoing note so that the echo returns at a lower pitch
switches from a constant note to a downward sweep as it nears prey
emits its calls through the mouth rather than the nostrils
lowers its call so the echo lands where its hearing is sharpest
detects fluttering insects by timing the gap between call and echo

proof.quote: lowers its outgoing note by just enough that the raised echo lands at the frequency where its hearing is sharpest

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says Schnitzler showed that a flying horseshoe bat lowers its outgoing note by just enough that the raised echo lands where its hearing is sharpest, the trick called Doppler shift compensation.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 7 says the bat lowers its note, and the echo comes back higher.
Mash-up: downward sweeps are the frequency-modulated calls of other bats earlier in paragraph 7.
Reversed: paragraph 7 says horseshoe bats emit through their nostrils.
Mash-up: timing the gap between call and echo is the distance method of paragraph 6, and Schnitzler's finding in paragraph 7 is about the pitch of the echo, not its timing.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if the small muscle in a bat's middle ear failed to relax after a call, the bat would most likely
choices: be deafened by the loudness of its own call
produce its next call at a lower pitch than usual
miss the faint echo that returns a moment later
produce a feeding buzz earlier than usual
receive echoes shifted higher in pitch than the call

proof.quote: relaxes within milliseconds so that the echo arrives at an ear that is open again
the bat must hear a faint echo a moment after shouting

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says the muscle contracts just before each call, damping the ear, and relaxes within milliseconds so the echo arrives at an ear that is open again. If it stayed contracted, the faint echo would arrive at a damped ear.
distractorNotes: Reversed: a muscle stuck in contraction keeps the ear damped, so the bat would hear less, not more.
Unrelated: paragraph 8 ties the muscle to hearing, not to the pitch of the next call.
Unrelated: the feeding buzz in paragraph 8 is driven by closing on prey, not by the ear muscle.
Wrong paragraph: the pitch shift is the Doppler effect of paragraph 7 and has nothing to do with the ear muscle.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the feeding buzz is
choices: a call rate of about ten per second used while a bat searches for prey
the loudest call a bat produces, exceeding 110 decibels
a burst of clicks that a tiger moth produces as a bat closes in
a steady note that a horseshoe bat holds while listening for Doppler shifts
a burst of up to 200 calls per second just before a bat reaches its prey

proof.quote: it rises to as many as 200 calls per second, a burst that researchers call the feeding buzz

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says that in the last fraction of a second before contact the rate rises to as many as 200 calls per second, a burst that researchers call the feeding buzz.
distractorNotes: Wrong phase: ten calls a second is the searching rate in paragraph 8, before prey is detected.
Mash-up: the 110 decibel figure in paragraph 8 is about loudness, not the rate of calls.
Wrong paragraph: clicks from tiger moths belong to paragraph 10.
Wrong paragraph: the steady note belongs to horseshoe bats in paragraph 7.

questions.stem: Which new situation best illustrates the principle described in paragraph 9?
choices: A deer that walks away from a faint wolf scent but bolts in wild zigzags when the scent grows strong
A rabbit that freezes in exactly the same way whether the sound it hears is faint or loud
A flock of birds that takes off together the instant a hawk appears, however far away it is
A fish that swims toward a faint vibration to investigate and flees only when the predator is in view
A squirrel that chatters loudly at a cat to warn the other squirrels before climbing a tree

proof.quote: the moth responds by turning and flying directly away
sets off something quite different: the moth folds its wings and drops, or breaks into loops and spirals that no echo can predict

questions.why: Paragraph 9's rule is a sensor with two thresholds: a faint signal means a distant threat and triggers an orderly move away, while a loud signal means a close threat and triggers wild, unpredictable evasion. The deer's calm retreat followed by zigzags is the same design.
distractorNotes: Wrong mechanism: paragraph 9 describes two different responses to faint and loud signals, not one response to everything.
Wrong mechanism: a single all-or-nothing response ignores the graded, two-threshold design of the moth's ear.
Reversed: the moth moves away from even a faint signal; it never approaches to investigate.
Wrong paragraph: signaling at a predator is the tiger moth idea of paragraph 10, not the two-cell ear of paragraph 9.

questions.stem: The author describes the 2009 experiment with Bertholdia trigona in paragraph 10 primarily to
choices: prove that tiger moth clicks serve only to jam a bat's sonar
show that Dunning and Roeder's 1965 result could not be repeated
explain how tiger moths produce clicks with their tymbals
offer evidence that fits jamming better than the other explanations
argue that big brown bats never learn to avoid moths that taste foul to them

proof.quote: a pattern that fits jamming rather than warning or startle
Three explanations have been offered, and they are not exclusive.

questions.why: Paragraph 10 presents three explanations and then says the Bertholdia trigona result, bats that kept trying and kept missing, fits jamming rather than warning or startle. The experiment is there to sort the explanations for that species.
distractorNotes: Too strong: paragraph 10 says the three explanations are not exclusive, and the finding is tied to one species.
Outside the passage: nothing says the 1965 result failed; the 2009 work asks why clicks work, not whether they do.
Wrong detail: how tymbals make clicks is explained earlier in paragraph 10, before the experiment.
Contradicted: paragraph 10 says bats learned to avoid clicking moths that tasted bad.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a palatable tiger moth that clicks is protected from bats because
choices: its clicks are too rapid for a bat to hear as separate sounds
its clicks startle bats, which never grow used to the sound
bats have come to associate clicking with a foul taste
it feeds as a caterpillar on plants that make it foul-tasting
its clicks clutter the moment when the echo is due

proof.quote: bats learned to avoid clicking moths that tasted bad, and then avoided palatable moths that clicked as well

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says bats learned to avoid clicking moths that tasted bad and then avoided palatable moths that clicked as well. The palatable moth is borrowing the lesson the bats learned from its foul-tasting relatives.
distractorNotes: Wrong mechanism: that is the jamming idea, which paragraph 10 ties to Bertholdia trigona, not to the palatable mimics.
Too extreme and wrong mechanism: the passage never says bats fail to get used to clicks, and the mimicry finding rests on learning.
Contradicted: the stem describes a palatable moth, so a foul taste cannot be the reason.
Wrong mechanism: jamming belongs to the 2009 experiment, not the 2007 mimicry result.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward describing the relationship between bats and moths as an arms race is best described as
choices: qualified acceptance
open hostility
unreserved enthusiasm
complete indifference
amused confusion

proof.quote: the metaphor is useful, but I distrust how neat it makes things

questions.why: Paragraph 11 says the arms race metaphor is useful but that the author distrusts how neat it makes things. That is a yes with a reservation attached: qualified acceptance.
distractorNotes: Too strong: the author calls the metaphor useful, which is not hostility.
Reversed: the author distrusts how neat the metaphor makes things, so the enthusiasm is anything but unreserved.
Wrong register: the author takes a position and explains it, which is the opposite of indifference.
Wrong register: there is no confusion in paragraph 11; the author names exactly what the metaphor leaves out.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Spallanzani's blinded bats proved in 1794 that bats navigate by sound, and later scientists merely confirmed what he had found
Echolocation in bats was suspected long before it could be shown, and its history reveals how much science depends on its instruments
Georges Cuvier's touch theory delayed the discovery of echolocation by more than a century and should serve as a warning against trusting authority
The defenses of eared moths and clicking tiger moths show that bats are steadily losing an evolutionary arms race with their prey
Donald Griffin's coining of the word echolocation in 1944 was the single most important event in the scientific study of bats

proof.quote: it took roughly 150 years to travel from a strong suspicion to an accepted fact
the answer was essentially in hand in the 1790s and nobody could hear it
how much a science depends on its instruments

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says the answer was essentially in hand in the 1790s and nobody could hear it, and paragraph 11 closes on how much a science depends on its instruments. The passage walks from suspicion to proof to mechanism and back to that lesson.
distractorNotes: Too strong: paragraph 3 says Spallanzani could not say how the ears worked, and paragraphs 5 to 10 are far more than confirmation.
Too narrow and against the author's view: paragraph 3 calls the tale of arrogance a little unfair.
Contradicted: paragraph 11 distrusts the arms race framing and says plenty of eared moths are eaten anyway.
Too extreme: coining the word is one event in paragraph 5, and the passage never ranks it above the rest.
